summary: Defines the Datamover Architecture for iSCSI, an abstract model separating the movement of data between iSCSI endpoints from the rest of the protocol so iSCSI can adapt to new transports. It does not define a specific protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Datamover Architecture lets iSCSI hand data movement to a separate layer while keeping control in the iSCSI layer. It describes how the two layers communicate, but not the wire protocol used by a Datamover.

questions: what are operational primitives in iscsi
subtitle: An architecture that separates iSCSI control from the movement of storage data.

tldr.problem: In the traditional iSCSI model, the iSCSI layer handles both protocol control and the movement of SCSI data, limiting how it can use transports that place data directly into a remote buffer.
tldr.mechanism: The Datamover Architecture separates data movement into a Datamover layer and defines abstract calls between that layer and iSCSI.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5047 defines an architecture, not a Datamover wire protocol. It has been updated by RFC 7146.

today: RFC 5047 is an Informational architecture document and has been updated by RFC 7146. It does not define a Datamover wire protocol.

sections.title: Why Separate Data Movement
sections.content:
iSCSI maps SCSI storage commands onto TCP/IP. In the traditional model, the iSCSI layer paces and performs the data transfer. Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) and Remote Direct Data Placement (RDDP) can place data directly in its final buffer on the remote node, avoiding a receive-side copy.

The Datamover Architecture (DA) separates the movement of data from the rest of iSCSI. This lets a Datamover use different data-placement or transport technologies while the iSCSI layer learns when an operation completes. The architecture is motivated by RDMA but does not depend on it.
sections.plainLanguage: DA lets one layer handle iSCSI commands and another move the data. This separation allows different transfer technologies to be used without changing the iSCSI layer's main job.

sections.title: The iSCSI and Datamover Layers
sections.content:
DA places a Datamover layer below iSCSI, with a Datamover Interface (DI) between them. The RFC shows RDMAP, DDP, MPA, and TCP as an example stack, but the architecture does not depend on those particular protocols.

The document defines the layers' responsibilities and how they communicate inside an end node. It does not define a new Datamover wire protocol or change the iSCSI wire protocol. A Datamover may be implemented in software or hardware, and the iSCSI session remains within the iSCSI layer.
sections.plainLanguage: The Datamover sits below iSCSI and uses a defined interface to receive work and report results. The architecture describes that interface, not the details of how data travels over the network.

sections.title: Data-Type and Control-Type Messages
sections.content:
DA divides iSCSI protocol data units (PDUs) into data-type and control-type groups. SCSI Data-In and Ready To Transfer (R2T) are data-type PDUs: they cause data to move without delivering the PDU itself to the remote iSCSI layer. Control-type PDUs include the remaining messages, including unsolicited SCSI Data-Out.

A Data_Descriptor identifies an I/O buffer. A Connection_Handle identifies a connection between local iSCSI and Datamover instances. An Operational Primitive is an abstract call that one layer uses to request an action from the other or report an event.

A Datamover protocol must provide reliable, in-order delivery, move data into or out of the I/O buffers, deliver control PDUs, and notify iSCSI when transfers finish or a connection ends.
sections.plainLanguage: Some PDUs carry instructions that iSCSI must read; others start data transfers that the Datamover can perform directly. The interface gives each connection and data buffer a way to be identified.

sections.title: Startup, Data Transfer, and Wrap-Up
sections.content:
At startup, the peers complete the ordinary iSCSI login. If they agree to use a Datamover, the iSCSI layer allocates connection resources and enables the Datamover. During the Full Feature Phase, communication for that connection goes through the Datamover.

The iSCSI layer uses calls such as Send_Control, Put_Data, and Get_Data. The Datamover reports control messages, transfer completion, acknowledgments, and connection failure through calls in the other direction. When a connection ends, the layers release their resources; on an unexpected failure the Datamover cleans up before notifying iSCSI.
sections.plainLanguage: The layers first agree to use the Datamover and set up its resources. During data transfer, iSCSI asks it to send or fetch data, and the Datamover reports completion or failure.

sections.title: Security and Resource Allocation
sections.content:
DA does not change the ordering and task rules of iSCSI. The security considerations for iSCSI therefore also apply to an implementation using this architecture. Each concrete Datamover protocol must describe its own security considerations.

The RFC identifies a denial-of-service risk if an implementation allocates Datamover resources too early. When login includes security negotiation, the iSCSI end node must wait until Login Operational Negotiation before allocating connection resources, so allocation follows authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Wait until the login security checks are complete before allocating Datamover resources. The architecture itself does not define a network protocol or replace iSCSI's security requirements.
